name: Grapeseed oil

card.summary: A linoleic-rich by-product of winemaking used as a light cosmetic and cooking oil, with no published trials on skin appearance.
card.note: Some batches have been found to contain polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons from seed drying.

quick.overview:
Grapeseed oil is pressed from the seeds left over from winemaking. It is mostly linoleic acid (omega-6), light in texture, and used in cooking, massage oils, cosmetics and hair-care products.

Reference sources say it contains negligible polyphenols, unlike the seeds themselves, and that clinical research has been too weak to show any reduction in disease risk. No clinical trials on skin appearance were found.
quick.mechanism: Linoleic acid is an essential fatty acid found in skin lipids, and topical linoleic-rich oils are a common emollient choice. The sources do not report mechanistic studies of grapeseed oil on skin. Studies compare its oxidative stability with other edible oils.
quick.risks: Reference sources note that the oil has occasionally been found to contain dangerous levels of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, likely from combustion gases during seed drying, and a 2000 study examined how processing affects this content. Its high polyunsaturated content makes it prone to oxidation.

lead: Grapeseed oil is a vegetable oil pressed from the seeds of grapes, a by-product of winemaking, with production concentrated in wine regions such as the Mediterranean.[1] It is mostly linoleic acid (about 70 percent), followed by oleic acid, with small amounts of vitamin E and plant sterols.[1] Its light texture and low odor make it a common base for facial and body oils, massage oils and hair products.[1][12]

People apply it to skin and hair as a lightweight emollient: the aim is smoother, more supple skin, a less greasy finish than heavier oils and shinier, softer hair. Formulation studies have loaded it into nanoemulgels and ionic-liquid emulsions to test effects on skin moisture, elasticity, pores and wrinkles.[13][14]

Reference sources state that, unlike the seeds, the oil contains negligible polyphenols, and that as of 2016 clinical research was too weak to show disease-risk reduction.[1] Small human studies of grapeseed oil formulations on facial skin exist, and an aromatherapy trial and several diet studies have used it as a base or test fat.[13][5]
infobox: Seeds of Vitis vinifera grapes (winemaking by-product)

paras: Winemaking accounts for about 90 percent of grape cultivation, and the seeds left after pressing can themselves be pressed for oil, which is why production is concentrated around the Mediterranean.[1] The oil is mainly sold refined for cooking and as a cosmetic carrier oil.

Typical fatty acid values are linoleic acid about 69.6 percent, oleic about 15.8, palmitic about 7 and stearic about 4, with trace alpha-linolenic acid. About 86 percent is unsaturated, so the omega-6 to omega-3 ratio is very high. Unsaponifiable matter of roughly 0.8 to 1.5 percent includes tocopherols and sterols such as beta-sitosterol, campesterol and stigmasterol.[1] Vitamin E is present in small amounts; safflower, cottonseed and rice bran oils contain more.[1] A study of 21 grape varieties found wide variation in oil composition, especially in linoleic acid and tocopherols.[1]

Wikipedia lists a food energy of 880 kcal per 100 g, an iodine value of 124 to 143 and a smoke point of about 216 C, higher than extra-virgin olive oil (193 C) and canola (204 C).[1] Linoleic acid is an essential fatty acid that occurs in skin lipids, which is why linoleic-rich oils are a common emollient choice.

Studies of edible-oil oxidation have compared grapeseed oil with other oils, and a food-science study used it in oleogels with beeswax.[3][4] Its high polyunsaturated fraction is generally associated with lower oxidative stability than monounsaturated oils, and cosmetic oils are usually stored cool and sealed.

In the kitchen the oil goes into dressings, mayonnaise and baked goods, serves as a base for oils infused with garlic, rosemary or spices, and is sprayed on raisins to help them keep their flavor.[1] For personal care it is used as a massage oil and as an ingredient in cosmetics and haircare, a use Wikipedia flags as needing a source.[1]

In the research literature the oil appears as a carrier in an aromatherapy trial for agitation in people with dementia, in an MRI breast-phantom design, and in diet studies of dietary fat and endotoxin or glycaemic response.[5][6][7][8]

A 2022 split-face, blinded, placebo-controlled study of 15 healthy volunteers tested a grapeseed oil nanoemulgel on the cheeks with weekly measurements over 12 weeks. The gel received higher sensory scores than placebo for appearance, color, odor, consistency and spreadability, and it significantly reduced melanin, erythema, sebum production and fine and large pores while increasing moisture and elasticity.[13] The authors noted that studies in disease conditions are still needed.

A 2024 paper in Pharmaceuticals combined grapeseed oil with a menthol-CoQ10 ionic liquid in a nanoscale emulsion (average size 218 nm). Skin penetration was 4.63 times that of an ordinary grapeseed oil emulsion in the lab, and after 28 days of use it increased stratum corneum water content and reduced transepidermal water loss and the count and length of under-eye lines, nasolabial folds and marionette lines.[14] A 2025 Scientific Reports study of fermented grapeseed oil reported better hair permeability than regular grapeseed oil or silicone oil in tests, and in vitro it delayed hair colour loss and improved mechanical properties of chemically damaged hair.[15] A 2023 review of nanotechnology for skin anti-aging lists many such carriers and actives.[16]

Reference sources state that the oil has occasionally been found to contain dangerous levels of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, likely from exposure to combustion gases when seeds are dried.[1] A 2000 study examined how processing affects PAH content in grapeseed oil.[2] A rat study reported that grapeseed oil modified diazinon-induced alterations.[9] Methods have been published to detect adulteration of the oil using near-infrared spectroscopy.[17]

The 2022 split-face trial of a grapeseed oil nanoemulgel, 15 volunteers over 12 weeks, is the main human skin study and measured melanin, erythema, sebum, pores, moisture and elasticity.[13] A 2007 Korean randomized trial of aromatherapy massage in post-menopausal women examined abdominal fat and body image; the two groups used different oils.[18]

Other human studies concern diet: a randomised crossover study of dietary fat and postprandial serum endotoxin,[7] and registered comparisons of dietary fats on vascular parameters (n=24) and on postprandial glucose, insulin and triglycerides.[10][11] A trial of aromatherapy for dementia-related agitation used the oil as a carrier rather than testing it.[5]
